entries.title: Garfield Park neighborhood shooting leaves man dead
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot in a West Side alley Tuesday morning. </p><p>The victim was in the alley in the 3400 block of West Polk Street, in the East Garfield Park neighborhood, when an assailant opened fire, shooting him multiple times, police and a fire department spokesperson said. </p><p>He was taken to Advocate Illinois Masonic Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead, according to police. His name, age and other personal information have not been released.</p><p>No arrests have been made. </p><p>Area 4 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Aficionados de Chicago se reúnen para el partido de la Copa del Mundo entre Estados Unidos y Bélgica
entries.summary: <p>En medio de la emoción y la controversia de la Copa del Mundo por la anulación de una tarjeta roja, los aficionados al fútbol se reunieron en masa el lunes en un bar del West Loop para ver el partido de Estados Unidos contra Bélgica.</p><p>Fanáticos de todas las edades —muchos equipados con camisetas, bufandas y banderas de Estados Unidos— llenaron el espacio al aire libre de Recess, ubicado en 838 W. Kinzie St., un lugar popular entre los aficionados al fútbol, en las horas previas al partido en el que Estados Unidos perdería 4-1 y sería eliminado de la Copa del Mundo.</p><p>Muchos dijeron que esperaban que Estados Unidos pudiera avanzar, tras el regreso al juego del jugador estrella Folarin Balogun, cuya tarjeta roja fue anulada en la victoria del equipo del 1 de julio sobre Bosnia y Herzegovina.</p><p>Otros expresaron su incomodidad con la forma en que se manejó la anulación de la tarjeta roja, después de que el presidente Donald Trump llamó al presidente de la FIFA para impugnarla.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-370000" name="module-370000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“¿Me gusta esa decisión como aficionado de Estados Unidos? No, pero así es el juego”, dijo Alec Santillán, de 28 años, de Jefferson Park, quien agregó que llegó a Recess por sugerencia de su hermano.</p><p>Santillán comentó que en general cree que las tarjetas rojas deberían mantenerse, a menos que sean claramente injustas. Pero, señaló, Balogun es un jugador fuerte y mejora al equipo.</p><p>Algunos aficionados tuvieron reacciones más contundentes en contra de que se mostrara la tarjeta roja en primer lugar.</p><p>“En ningún momento pensé que merecía una tarjeta roja”, dijo Kathryn Hemingway, residente de Rogers Park de 53 años y titular de un boleto de temporada del Chicago Fire.</p><div class="Enhancement" Pero definitivamente estoy animando a Estados Unidos”, comentó.</p><p>Maggie McDevitt, de 22 años, expresó que pensaba que la tarjeta roja era “realmente estúpida”.</p><p>Como jugadora de fútbol, el movimiento en cuestión, en el que Balogun pisó el tobillo de otro jugador, parecía “obviamente involuntario”.</p><p>“Jugando desde atrás, eso me ha ocurrido muchas veces, y los árbitros generalmente ni siquiera lo notan”, dijo McDevitt.</p><p>McDevitt es de Filadelfia y se graduó en primavera del programa de enfermería de la Universidad Loyola. Ella y sus amigos eligieron Recess para ver el partido mientras celebraban el cumpleaños número 22 de su amiga.</p><p>Aun así, dijo que está más enfocada en el juego en sí que en la controversia política.</p><p>Algunos viajaron lejos para ver el partido en Chicago.</p><p>Pranav Reddy, de 27 años, vino desde Nueva Jersey para visitar a su hermano y ver el juego.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Illinois health officials warn of high rate of intestinal illness caused by contaminated foods
entries.summary: <p>State health officials are warning the public about a heightened number of cases of the intestinal illness cyclosporiasis following an even larger outbreak in Michigan.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Public Health has reported 141 cases of the illness, which is most often contracted by consuming contaminated foods.</p><p>In Michigan, more than 700 people have become ill with cyclosporiasis since June 22, according to the Michigan Department of Public Health.</p><p>The most common symptoms of the illness are diarrhea, nausea, fatigue, loss of appetite, weight loss, cramping and bloating, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.</p><p>Treatments include resting and drinking plenty of fluids, as well as antibiotics, according to the CDC.</p><p>The best practices to prevent cyclosporiasis include washing your hands before eating, washing all fruits and vegetables before eating, cutting or cooking, and refrigerating cut, peeled, or cooked fruits and vegetables as soon as possible, according to the CDC.</p><p>Prior to most of the Illinois cases and the Michigan outbreak, the CDC had reported 145 cases of cyclosporiasis between May 1 and June 16 in 17 states across the U.S. Twenty of those people were hospitalized, and no cases resulted in death, the CDC said.</p>

entries.title: Pepe Vargas, campeón del cine latino, anuncia su retiro y un nuevo liderazgo en las artes multiculturales
entries.summary: <p>Pepe Vargas nunca imaginó retirarse.</p><p>Después de décadas liderando el International Latino Cultural Center, el director ejecutivo y fundador, Vargas renunció el pasado martes por razones de salud. La organización, que ha sido guardiana del arte y de artistas panlatinos en Chicago durante más de 40 años, continuará bajo un nuevo liderazgo.</p><p>Mateo Mulcahy, quien ha estado en el centro cultural desde 2022, es el nuevo director ejecutivo del centro. Y con un nuevo liderazgo vienen nuevas metas, incluida la esperanza de encontrar un espacio físico para recibir visitantes y organizar eventos, como cualquier otra institución cultural en la ciudad.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7d0000" name="module-7d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Vargas, que cumplió 78 años el día en que renunció, es uno de los líderes de arte latino más antiguos de Chicago, comparable a Carlos Tortolero, fundador del Museo Nacional de Arte Mexicano (NMMA) en Pilsen, y Myrna Salazar, fundadora de la Alianza de Teatro Latino de Chicago. Tortolero <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2023/11/15/23962615/fundador-del-museo-nacional-de-arte-mexicano-se-jubila-despues-de-36-anos" target="_blank" >se retiró</a> en 2023, mientras que Salazar <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2022/8/5/23293880/myrna-salazar-muere-a-los-75-anos-cofundadora-de-la-alianza-de-teatro-latino-chicago-espanol-la-voz" target="_blank" >falleció a los 75 años en 2022</a>. (Vargas fue uno de los cuatro fundadores del grupo de teatro, una lista que incluía a Carlos Hernández de la Alianza de Artes Puertorriqueñas.)</p><p>Vargas ayudó a dar forma al centro cultural y, en muchos aspectos, al panorama más amplio de la vida cultural latina en Chicago, desde el crecimiento del Festival de Cine Latino hasta su vasto programa cultural por el que es conocido hoy.</p><p>El trabajo que realizó fue lo que lo mantuvo “lleno de energía” y “devoto” durante más de 40 años. Nacido y criado en La Mesa, un pequeño pueblo en Colombia a unas dos horas de Bogotá, Vargas llegó a Chicago en 1980.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d93ddf" name="image-d93ddf"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e5d3ea8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1920x1078+0+1/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F24%2F18%2Ff4cf020c4eedbec3a292cafa89aa%2Fmexico-i-am-frankelda.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/890bcf1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1920x1078+0+1/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F24%2F18%2Ff4cf020c4eedbec3a292cafa89aa%2Fmexico-i-am-frankelda.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1d46dfc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1920x1078+0+1/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F24%2F18%2Ff4cf020c4eedbec3a292cafa89aa%2Fmexico-i-am-frankelda.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Pepe Vargas convirtió el Festival Latino de Cine en una plataforma destacada para cineastas. El festival de este año presentó “Soy Frankelda”, el primer largometraje en stop-motion realizado íntegramente en suelo mexicano.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided/Chicago Latino Film Festival</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Estudió periodismo de difusión en Columbia College Chicago y se graduó con el deseo de hacer cortometrajes y documentales. Luego, en 1985, el amante del cine Vargas lanzó el Festival de Cine Latino de Chicago, que ahora es el más grande y de mayor duración en los Estados Unidos.</p><p>Ese primer evento, con solo 14 películas, evolucionó hacia el Chicago Latino Cinema, que más tarde se convirtió en la organización sin fines de lucro hoy como ILCC. Este año, el <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/13/el-festival-de-cine-latino-de-chicago-lleva-a-los-cinefilos-a-mexico-venezuela-cuba-y-mas-alla" target="_blank" >festival de cine celebró su 42.º aniversario</a>.</p><p>Vargas dijo que creó la organización para combatir el racismo y la discriminación a través del arte. “Es el impacto”, comentó. Vargas mencionó que él y el equipo de liderazgo siempre tuvieron un entendimiento mutuo de “lo vital que es para nosotros realmente tener una manera de tener voz, de empoderar a nuestra gente para pensar, y de realmente aprovechar las muchas diferencias que existen entre nosotros… cuando juntamos eso, realmente nos convertimos en una comunidad poderosa”.</p><p>Vargas dijo que no tiene arrepentimientos sobre haberle dado a la organización cultural todo lo que pudo y que se divirtió “mucho” haciéndolo.</p><p>“La gente pasa su vida pensando, planeando y ahorrando, en lugar de vivir el momento”, señaló. “Hago mi mejor esfuerzo y lo he hecho a lo largo de los años para [vivir] en el presente”.</p><p>Jorge Valdivia, el director ejecutivo de la Alianza de Teatro Latino de Chicago (CLATA), dijo que siempre ha apreciado a Vargas por el trabajo que hizo con el festival de cine cada año.</p><p>Ambos no siempre estaban de acuerdo, pero Valdivia dijo que aprecia la capacidad de disentir en algunas cosas.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3177f3" creo que como individuos, dice mucho sobre tu humanidad cuando puedes sentarte en la misma sala con alguien y escuchar su opinión”, expresó Valdivia, quien trabajó con Vargas en el comité directivo de la Cumbre Anual de Artes y Cultura Latina de Chicago.</p><p>Y mientras que el festival de cine de este año trajo más de 80 películas de largometraje y cortometrajes de toda América Latina, España, Portugal y el Caribe, el grupo también organiza una variedad de otros eventos que celebran las tradiciones artísticas panlatinas, muchos de los cuales se han ampliado gracias a las contribuciones de Mulcahy.</p><p>Eso incluye la serie musical Levitt VIBE Chicago. La alineación de conciertos de 10 semanas de esta temporada comenzó en junio con actuaciones en el Parque Riis de Belmont Cragin hasta el 22 de agosto. Las Guaracheras, un grupo de chicas de Colombia, se presentan el 18 de julio, mientras que varios artistas venezolanos aparecerán el 25 de julio para una noche de herencia.</p><p>La organización también alberga un Club de Cine Reel mensual en Facets y un programa anual de Films in the Parks (que comienza el 8 de julio y se repite durante cinco semanas cada miércoles). También ya están en marcha los planes para el Festival de Danza Latino de Chicago en otoño.</p><p>Apartarse de todo esto se sintió “inconcebible” para Vargas. Pero los recientes <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/06/24/pepe-vargas-se-retira-dejando-un-gran-legado-en-chicago-me-voy-absolutamente-satisfecho-de-lo-que-hice" target="_blank" >problemas de salud han puesto todo en una nueva perspectiva, como reportó La Voz</a>.</p><p>“Creo que lo más importante fue crear un equipo de personas que se hicieran cargo en caso de que fuera necesario”, comentó Vargas. “Y, bueno, llegó el momento”.</p><p>Mulcahy, un originario de Chicago de ascendencia mexicana e irlandesa, ha trabajado en la organización desde enero de 2022 class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Antes de unirse al centro cultural, Mulcahy trabajó en la Old Town School of Folk Music como director de proyectos comunitarios y de eventos.</p><p>Valdivia dijo que está emocionado por la próxima “evolución” del centro cultural bajo el liderazgo de Mulcahy.</p><p>A medida que Vargas se retira, se refiere a Mulcahy como su “mano derecha”. Y a lo largo de los años, ambos han colaborado para consolidar y ampliar la visión progresista del centro cultural.</p><p>Eso incluye una búsqueda “activa” para adquirir un hogar permanente más allá de un pequeño espacio de oficina en el Loop, dijo Mulcahy. Anteriormente, el grupo operaba desde un aula del Instituto Cervantes, que ofrece clases de español.</p><p>Pero Vargas dijo que imagina ese espacio como una “catedral” para las artes panlatinas, donde los visitantes pueden entrar y salir.</p><p>“Sentimos que podemos ser más efectivos y conservar a más personas a través de nuestro propio espacio”, dijo Mulcahy. El espacio se construirá sobre los siete pilares de la organización: cine, música, danza, teatro, artes culinarias, artes visuales y artes literarias.</p><p>Como hombre retirado, Vargas dijo que espera asistir a los eventos del centro cultural como invitado. Él dice que Chicago lo convirtió en “una persona destacada”. Y eventualmente, después de recibir el visto bueno de su médico, espera regresar a Colombia.</p><p>“Aun con todos los problemas y percances políticos, [es] un paraíso”, dijo. “Iré con un sentido diferente de apreciación, comenzando una nueva vida”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Underground storage project aims to fix chronic flooding in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Acknowledging the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/04/10/flooding-chicago-climate-change-deep-tunnel-mold-metropolitan-water-reclamation-district-soaked" >city’s persistent flooding problem</a>, Mayor Brandon Johnson, flanked by other elected officials Tuesday, touted a West Side pilot project aimed at temporarily capturing rain underground before it can overwhelm Chicago’s outdated sewers.</p><p>The city is splitting the $12 million cost to build the underground storage along two streets in Austin with the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District, the government body that controls stormwater flooding and treats sewage.</p><p>The pilot sites are on a stretch of West Le Moyne Street west of North Laramie Avenue, where the news conference took place, and a recently completed area of West Maypole Street immediately west of North Cicero Avenue. The Le Moyne project is expected to be completed by fall.</p><p>The West Side, where Johnson owns a home, experienced historic floods in 2023 due to a combination of storms intensified by climate change and aging sewer infrastructure that should have been replaced.</p><p>Designed many decades ago, Chicago’s sewers can handle 2 inches of rain in a 24-hour period before flooding becomes likely. The storms of 2023 dumped 8 to 9 inches of rain over short periods of time. About a month’s worth of rain was dumped across Chicago during the recent July Fourth weekend.</p><p>“We can only expect more storms to come as the effects of climate change hit Chicago’s communities,” Johnson said at a news conference in Austin. “And, of course, they hit the South and West side communities especially harder. It is well past time to update and modernize our infrastructure and build a city that works for everyone.”</p><p>Some <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/06/17/west-side-residents-wait-aging-sewers-homes-damaged-2023-floods" >West Side residents are still hoping</a> for the city to provide financial assistance to fix damaged homes — in part from more than $520 million Johnson has vowed to spend. But on Tuesday the mayor focused on flood prevention.</p><p>“This approach is to build for the future, as we know the infrastructure here in Chicago has not had a significant upgrade in decades,” Johnson said.</p><p>While suburban areas with more open land can provide more options for flood control with added green space, solutions for Chicago’s neighborhoods, especially on the West Side, pose challenges.</p><p>The floodwater storage is being built with 12-by-12-foot concrete sections that weigh 48,000 pounds each, according to Randy Conner, commissioner of the Department of Water Management.</p><p>“Adding infrastructure in dense urban neighborhoods is like putting pieces of a puzzle together,” Conner said.</p><p>About 50 to 60 sections are being installed on each block just under street level.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" data-align-center> <a class="AnchorLink" Chicago’s Deep Tunnel sends floodwaters through more than 100 miles of tunnels into three reservoirs. Built over a half-century, the system was created to protect Lake Michigan and other waterways as well as help prevent flooding.</p><p>The news conference followed the announcement a day earlier that the massive Deep Tunnel suburban reservoirs were nearly full after a month of heavy rain. The problem pointed to the need for additional flood control.</p><p>Those reservoirs were still mostly full Tuesday.</p><p>“There’s no one silver bullet,” said Kari Steele, board president of the water reclamation district.</p><p>As for concerns about the flood-control reservoirs nearing full capacity, Steele defended the multibillion dollar civil engineering plan, saying, “It is doing exactly what it was designed to do.”</p><p>Scientists have predicted more intense storms in the coming years, which adds pressure on planners and politicians charged with keeping people safe during extreme weather events. Johnson said that became clear to him after the 2023 floods.</p><p>“As I said three years ago, these 100-year storms were going to become more and more regular,” Johnson said.</p><div entries.title: U.S. men's national soccer team again fails to make significant progress
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — For all the growth in American soccer over the past quarter-century, the U.S. men's national team remains stagnant.</p><p>Christian Pulisic, Tyler Adams and Weston McKennie fared no better at the World Cup in 2022 and 2026 than Tim Howard, Michael Bradley and Jozy Altidore did in 2010 and 2014.</p><p>"We want to be able to go and compete with some of the best in the world and we just still have that next step to come," Pulisic said after Monday night's error-filled <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/soccer/2026/07/06/world-cup-us-belgium" >4-1 loss to Belgium</a> in the round of 16.</p><p>For all the billions of dollars invested with the goal of boosting the national team into the world's elite, the Americans remain soccer plebians.</p><p>After reaching the semifinals of the first World Cup in 1930, the U.S. didn't even qualify between 1950 and 1990. Since then, the Americans were eliminated in the round of 16 in 1994, 2010, 2014, 2022 and this year, failed to advance past their group in 1990, 1998 and 2006, and flopped in qualifying for 2018.</p><p>"It's not like you are in a rocket and you improve and you grow. ... It's not linear," U.S. coach Mauricio Pochettino said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/soccer/2026/07/06/world-cup-us-belgium" >U.S. booted from World Cup after 4-1 loss to Belgium</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/07/07/us-belgium-world-cup-most-watched-soccer-telecast-in-us-history-fox" >U.S.-Belgium World Cup match is most-watched soccer telecast in U.S. history, Fox says</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/07/06/chicago-fans-us-belgium-world-cup-recess" >Chicago fans turn out for U.S., Belgium World Cup match</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The U.S. won three games in a World Cup for the first time, beating Paraguay, Australia and Bosnia-Herzegovina while losing to Turkey and Belgium. The Americans benefited as host, a seeded team that didn't face a top-10 nation before the Red Devils.</p><p>By the next World Cup in Spain, Portugal and Morocco (with three games in South America), Pulisic, McKennie and Adams will be 31.</p><h3>Which players increased value for the U.S. national team?</h3><p>Folarin Balogun led the U.S. team with three goals, looking like a top striker, and gained worldwide notoriety when his red card suspension for awkwardly landing on an opponent's ankle was lifted after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/soccer/2026/07/06/trump-fifa-actions-around-folarin-balogun-suspension-puts-world-cup-integrity-in-question" >a phone call from U.S. President Donald Trump.</a> A former Arsenal youth player, the 25-year-old striker is entering the fourth season of a five-year contract with French club Monaco and could be set for a move to a bigger club.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">MALIK TILLMAN FORCES THE EQUALIZER FOR THE <a href="https://x.com/USMNT?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@USMNT</a> 🇺🇸<br><br>ANOTHER FREE KICK BEAUTY AND THE BUILDING SHAKES IN SEATTLE! <a href="https://t.co/uUO9amIJ3Z">pic.twitter.com/uUO9amIJ3Z</a></p>— FOX Sports (@FOXSports) <a href="https://x.com/FOXSports/status/2074290520235417737?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 7, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Malik Tillman became the first player since France's Bernard Genghini in 1982 to have two free kick goals in a World Cup. The 24-year-old midfielder is entering the second season of a five-year contract with German club Bayer Leverkusen. He had a difficult 2025-26, getting dropped from the starting lineup between late March and the season's final match.</p><h3>Does U.S. coach Mauricio Pochettino stay in the job for another four years?</h3><p>Pochettino said he will speak with the U.S. Soccer Federation after a rest period to discuss whether it wants him to stay beyond the expiration of his contract this summer and whether he wants to commit to a four-year cycle.</p><p>"We had positive conversations with Mauricio before the World Cup about the future. We agreed we would continue those conversations following a chance to rest and reflect post World Cup," the U.S. Soccer Federation said in a statement Tuesday. "We have a great deal of respect and gratitude for Mauricio, his staff and everyone part of the program. We have shared excitement about our potential and also shared clarity about the amount of work at all levels still required to achieve our ambition."</p><p>The Argentine took over from Gregg Berhalter in late 2024 after first-round elimination at the Copa America. His first year included failures to win the CONCACAF Gold Cup and Nations League.</p><p>"We were in a mess," he said. "I've seen this team show that we can play football. We can play soccer. We can compete. That we need keep improving — a lot of young players with a lot potential and future."</p><h3>Trouble spots on the field need work for the national team</h3><p>Goalkeeper has gone from the United States' biggest strength from 1990 through 2014 to a huge weakness in the past decade and appears to be at its weakest since the 1980s.</p><p>Long gone are the days when Tony Meola, Kasey Keller, Brad Friedel, Tim Howard and Brad Guzan inspired confidence.</p><p>Zack Steffen and Matt Turner both failed to establish themselves with big European teams. Matt Freese, who supplanted Turner as the first-choice starter last year, gifted a goal in the loss to Belgium that will be replayed on blooper reels.</p><p>Gabriel Slonina, Chris Brady, Patrick Schulte and Roman Celentano, who head the next generation, have the next cycle to establish themselves as possible No. 1s.</p><p>Central defense also is a concern. Crystal Palace's Chris Richards is the only American playing at a top club and his World Cup partner, Tim Ream, at 38 became the oldest U.S. player at any World Cup.</p><h3>Qualifying should be easier with 48-team World Cup tournaments</h3><p>With the expansion of the field to 48 nations, including six from North and Central America and the Caribbean, World Cup qualifying is not likely to be challenging for CONCACAF's powers: Mexico, the U.S. and Canada.</p><p>All three were eliminated in the round of 16 after Curaçao, Haiti and Panama were eliminated with last-place finishes in their groups.</p><p>Unless the U.S. shows vast improvement, it will not be seeded for the 2030 World Cup and likely will face a world power in the first round.<br></p>

entries.title: U.S.-Belgium World Cup match is most-watched soccer telecast in U.S. history, Fox says
entries.summary: <p>The U.S. game against Belgium in the round of 16 at the World Cup set another record as the most-watched soccer telecast in U.S. history, Fox said after preliminary ratings came out Tuesday.</p><p>Fox said 30 million people watched the game, a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/soccer/2026/07/06/world-cup-us-belgium" > 4-1 victory for Belgium </a>on Monday in Seattle to move into the quarterfinals and eliminate the last of the tournament's three co-hosts. Fox said audience peaked at more than 36.8 million people between 9:15 and 9:30 p.m. Eastern Time.</p><p>That topped the previous mark, the U.S.-Bosnia-Herzegovina game last week that Fox said was watched by 26.4 million.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/soccer/2026/07/06/world-cup-us-belgium" >U.S. booted from World Cup after 4-1 loss to Belgium</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/07/06/chicago-fans-us-belgium-world-cup-recess" >Chicago fans turn out for U.S., Belgium World Cup match</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Police share video of man wanted for killing CTA employee
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police have released video of a man they believe shot and killed a CTA employee last week.</p><p>Kevin Barlow, 57, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/29/god-has-taken-his-angel-friends-and-family-mourn-cta-worker-fatally-shot-in-roseland" target="_blank" >fatally shot during a carjacking</a> around 4 a.m. June 29 in the 9800 block of South State Street, outside the 98th Street rail maintenance facility.</p><p>In a video published by Chicago police on Tuesday, the suspect is shown walking on several different surveillance video angles wearing dark pants and a gray hoodie with a Chicago Bears claw logo on the back. The video also shows him walking from the area near West 97th Street and South Michigan Avenue to the block where the shooting happened, and then later in the 10100 block of South Perry Avenue.</p><p>Anyone with information can call CPD detectives on the case at 312-747-8271.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/jauG6oNvWSo?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Homicide | DISTRICT 05 |June 29, 2026 I Chicago Police Department"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Man sentenced to 6 years in $1.2 million tech help fraud scheme
entries.summary: <p>A man has been sentenced to six years in federal prison for defrauding people of $1.2 million with a banking tech help scheme, according to the U.S. Attorney’s office for the Northern District of Illinois.</p><p>Kartik Saini, 33, was handed a sentence of six years and a month in federal prison by U.S. District Judge John Robert Blakey on June 25, according to the office.</p><p>In 2020 and 2021, he and others acted as employees of Google, Apple, Citibank and other companies to tell victims their accounts or computers had been hacked, prosecutors said. They then told the victims they needed to wire money in the form of gift cards or cryptocurrency to the companies for safekeeping.</p><p>In total, they took $1.2 million from four victims, including $746,000 from a Chicago woman, which prosecutors said made up “a large portion of her retirement savings.”</p><p>Saini was arrested in New York in August 2024 when he arrived on a flight from India. He pleaded guilty in March to a charge of wire fraud.</p>

entries.title: How homeowners can reduce flood risk as retention reservoirs approach capacity
entries.summary: <p>Experts say homeowners should consider proven tips to reduce their flood risk as Chicago's retention reservoirs approach capacity and more rain is forecast later this week.</p><p>“We need to be prepared for [flooding] all the time, maybe a little more prepared now because we have less room for heavy rain,” says Scott Lincoln, senior service hydrologist at the Chicago branch of the National Weather Service.</p><p>Some parts of the Chicago area have seen 8 inches of rain since the beginning of July, nearly a third of what the area typically gets in a year, Lincoln said. As a result, Deep Tunnel, the network of floodwater management, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/06/chicago-deep-tunnel-historic-flooding-tarp-reservoir-weather-climate-change" target="_blank" >has never been as full as it is now</a>.</p><p>More rain is forecast Thursday and Friday, which could potentially overload the network and cause flooding. The south suburbs are especially at risk.</p><p>Ideally, residents would have certain flood precautions in place already, Lincoln said, but there are things that can be done before more rain comes.</p><p>Here are some of those tips:</p><p></p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/06/chicago-deep-tunnel-historic-flooding-tarp-reservoir-weather-climate-change" target="_blank" ></a></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><h3>Downspout redirection</h3><p>The best way to mitigate flood risk is to redirect the downspout that brings water from rain gutters directly into the sewer. Moving the downspout output to a garden or other landscaping relieves the sewer system during heavy rain.</p><p>“Downspouts directly connect water from roofs to the sewer system, so during heavy rains the rain from all the roofs in an area reduces capacity in the sewer system" and can lead to sewer backup and flooding, Cyatharine Alias, urban resilience director at Center for Neighborhood Technology, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/04/10/flooding-chicago-climate-change-deep-tunnel-mold-metropolitan-water-reclamation-district-soaked" target="_blank" >told the Sun-Times earlier this year</a>.</p><p>Homeowners can redirect their downspout by using a hacksaw to shorten the downspout, then add an extension that directs the water where you want it to go. TikTok and YouTube tutorials can be helpful, but remember not to direct water toward others’ property. The Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago has a step-by-step guide to disconnecting a downspout in its <a class="Link" href="https://mwrd.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/Green_Neighbor_Guide_250220.pdf" target="_blank" >Green Neighbor Guide</a>.</p><h3>Rain barrels</h3><p>Rain barrels can also help prevent water from seeping into homes. Hardware and garden stores often keep rain barrels in stock, and Cook County residents can buy directly from the MWRD, whose barrels are $22.30 or $11.15 for those 65 and older. Tips on rain barrel installation can also be found in the Green Neighbor Guide.</p><h3>Water conservation and landscaping</h3><p>The MWRD suggests conserving water by doing simple things like taking shorter showers and turning off the water while brushing your teeth. Flushing anything other than natural waste and toilet paper can cause plumbing backups that can contribute to water issues.</p><p>The district also recommends investing in green infrastructure, like replacing paved areas with pervious surfaces to mitigate the effects of flooding. Planting a rain garden and landscaping with native plants can help the ecosystem thrive even under heavy rain and ward off flooding.</p><h3>Navigating flood effects and staying informed</h3><p>Because the streams, rivers and reservoirs in the area are elevated after heavy rain last week, it won’t take much more precipitation for them to flood, said Lincoln, of the Weather Service.</p><p>In the event that floods do happen, Lincoln said staying up to date on the most recent developments in your area is important. Having multiple sources of information can help residents get the information that’s most pertinent to them, especially when it comes to transportation.</p><p>“We definitely want people to think about, 'Do they have multiple ways to get to work?'” Lincoln said. “What do you do if the main road is blocked?”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://mwrd.org/community-action/overflow-action" target="_blank" >MWRD Overflow Action Alerts</a> can warn residents of storms and help them remember to conserve water before, during and after a storm. Local governments often post on social media or send email alerts regarding severe weather and flooding risks along with tips to manage heavy rain.</p>
entries.author: Mary Norkol

entries.title: Ups and downs: Hard way to fly — or to win World Series — but Cubs tout ability to move on from highs, lows
entries.summary: <p>BALTIMORE — Coming in for a landing, my plane slammed down on the runway.</p><p>By the time the person sitting next to me lifted the window shade, we were back in the air.</p><p>Ten minutes later? Back on the ground.</p><p>It’s not the ideal way to fly.</p><p>When the flight attendant — playing to the heavy contingent of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> fans aboard — signed off with, ‘‘Let’s go, Cubbies!’’ it struck me that this was maybe not the ideal way to go through a baseball season, either.</p><p>But the up-and-down Cubs are making a run at it, trying to achieve their sky-high goals, all while their season has — to this point, anyway — jerked upward and downward with the frequency of a commercial jet.</p><p>You know the highs and lows by now. A 10-game winning streak. Then another. Then a 10-game losing streak to kick off a monthlong slump. Then the bats roared back to life.</p><p>They <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/01/cubs-dansby-swanson-home-runs-rbis-padres-offense-lineup-craig-counsell-nico-hoerner-pete-crow-armstrong-michael-conforto" target="_blank" >won a game by 20 runs</a>. They <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/03/cubs-have-one-of-those-days-in-17-1-loss-to-cardinals" target="_blank" >lost the next by 16</a>.</p><p>Whiplash, anyone?</p><p>These Cubs say they’re equipped to handle such a season, constantly trumpeting their ability to show up to the ballpark each new day having forgotten about the emotional highs and lows of the previous one.</p><p>That they held the top wild-card spot in the National League when that flight took off Tuesday shows they might be right.</p><p>They’re taking Ted Lasso’s advice and selling this roster as a collection of 26 goldfish.</p><p>‘‘In the first six weeks of the season or eight weeks of the season,’’ outfielder Ian Happ said Tuesday, ‘‘just the ups and downs of that certainly made it more important to understand that whether we win 10 in a row or lose 10 in a row, one two-week stretch isn’t going to determine whether we have a great year or not.’’</p><p>This might sound like Baseball 101. But considering how fans’ emotions have swung wildly between high and low during the Cubs’ numerous streaks and stretches, the guys actually going through it must be feeling something, right? They must be battling some sort of human nature to put weight on the moment, right?</p><p>How does one learn to wipe away what came immediately before in service of the now?</p><p>‘‘A baseball season teaches you to do that,’’ manager Craig Counsell said, ‘‘because you can have an emotional game end at 11 o’clock [one night] and there’s another game at 1 o’clock the next day. You get taught to do it through that.</p><p>‘‘In that sense, the game’s a really good teacher, and you learn that it’s required of you pretty fast, whether it’s a consistent season or a really streaky season.’’</p><p>You know who else were good teachers, at least for one Cubs player? The guys with rings on their fingers.</p><p>Happ made his major-league debut the season after the Cubs rode into Grant Park to celebrate winning the 2016 World Series and learned from players who had been to the mountaintop and knew what it took to get there.</p><p>Now he’s the connective tissue between that team and the one chasing a similar goal.</p><p>‘‘You have to be ready for the next day, and dwelling on what happened the day prior doesn’t really help,’’ he said. ‘‘You learn it when you’re young from veteran players. I learned it from that group that I came up with that had a ton of experience and won at the highest stage. You learn from those guys and kind of carry that forward.</p><p>‘‘It’s more from actions and coming to work every day. There’s definitely times when [someone is] going through something where some words help, just [letting them know that a] one-week stretch or two-week stretch isn’t going to define the season.’’</p><p>Experience can be a pretty effective teacher, too. And though they didn’t plan it, the Cubs now have the experience of riding through a streaky few months.</p><p>Can they use it to their advantage as the summer goes on? We soon will find out.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: Chicago midyear budget claims $131.7M shortfall
entries.summary: <p>Last January, Mayor Brandon Johnson said he was already preparing City Hall for a potentially painful round of midyear layoffs if revenue fell short, infuriating the rebel bloc that muscled an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/12/19/chicago-city-council-approves-alternate-revenue-plan-minus-mayor-brandon-johnsons-corporate-head-tax" target="_blank" >alternative budget</a> through the City Council after rejecting Johnson’s corporate head tax.</p><p>Now, the mayor has what he views as black-and-white proof that his dire prediction has come true — without saying what he intends to do about it.</p><p>The midyear budget report shows that the alternative revenues approved by renegade alderpersons over Johnson’s strenuous objections have fallen $131.7 million short of projections.</p><p>The sale of long-term city debt was expected to generate $89.6 million, but it has so far produced zero.</p><p>The sale of city advertising has come up empty even though it was supposed to rake in $29.3 million.</p><p>Johnson’s decision to join forces with Bally’s and continue fighting the decision to lift the Chicago ban on video gambling terminals has put the city $6.8 million further in the hole.</p><p>Same goes for the anticipated $6 million expected to be generated by an augmented reality licensing program. That's a technology that overlays virtual elements into the real world through devices like smartphones and smart glasses.</p><p>On Tuesday, the mayor who has never stopped fighting the budget battle he lost essentially said, “I told you so.”</p><p>“We had a pathway that would have avoided this. Had City Council accepted the $100 million from the top corporate earners … we wouldn’t be in this predicament right now. So hopefully, it’s a lesson learned by certain members of City Council because these challenges won’t disappear in one budget,” he said.</p><p>"We did not need to cede to big-money interests and fall back on the tired practice of balancing budgets on the backs of working people."</p><p>The show-and-tell presentation did not answer the most important question: what the mayor intends to do to erase the $131.7 million midyear shortfall.</p><p>He would only say Tuesday that he is “working hard to avoid cutting services and layoffs” and urging the City Council to avoid "reverting back to a style” of budget balancing that has “left working families in absolute peril." </p><p>"Every single progressive revenue source that I put forward is over-performing,” Johnson said.</p><p>“The progressive movement is alive and well. We just have a few obstinate individuals that are more aligned with the interests of corporations that are ultimately stalling what could be a full-out revolution in this city. And the people in Chicago want it. They want it desperately."</p><p>Southwest Side Ald. Matt O’Shea (19th) was a leading member of the renegade group that waged a budget rebellion not seen since the 1980s power struggle known as Council Wars.</p><p>O’Shea accused the mayor of “sabotaging” the alternative, $16.7 billion budget to make his doomsday scenario come true.</p><p>“We designed a budget that the administration had to execute. These are his own people that he put in place who failed to execute. He needs to look within. Once again, as we’ve seen for the past 3.5 years, he fails and continues to fail,” O’Shea told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“We’re now midyear, and he’s failed to execute much of the budget that was passed. That’s on him. ... It’s another example of his failure to — of his administration to — execute. That’s what this is. … He’s saying 'I failed to lead, so I’m gonna go back to the same lines that I’ve always gone with’: Tax the rich and implement plans that the overwhelming majority of not only the City Council but taxpayers don’t want to see.”</p><p>If Johnson follows that now-familiar political script, O’Shea said Chicago is headed for a pre-election repeat of the budget rebellion that saw the battle of the budget drag on until days before Christmas.</p><p>“I would only hope that the great collaborator wants to sit down and work with us this time, unlike last time. If he doesn’t, then once again, you’ll see the City Council be the adults in the room,” O’Shea said.</p><p>The 31-member group including O’Shea that calls itself the “Budget Accountability Coalition” issued a statement saying its sole focus is to put the city on “the best financial footing possible in the wake of Johnson administration actions that have led to credit downgrades and ballooning budget deficits.”</p><p>“Instead of executing the financially sound budget that City Council passed last year, Mayor Johnson and his administration have spent six months slow-walking the implementation of new revenues and efficiencies designed to close our budget deficit and prevent this administration from creating excuses to raise taxes on businesses, jobs, and working families and skip the remainder of our advance pension payment,” the statement said.</p><p>“Chicagoans deserve transparency and the truth from the mayor instead of attempts to shift blame away from the failures of his administration.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago Park District's Adventure Club opens the outdoors to those with disabilities
entries.summary: <p>Alex Stanley, 31, never went fishing before Tuesday.</p><p>Now he has, thanks to Adventure Club, a Chicago Park District program that brings dozens of children and adults to Northerly Island every summer to try new outdoor activities.</p><p>"I like being here," said Stanley, who was attending Adventure Club for the first time. "Everything's fun for me."</p><p>Stanley said he had experience hiking during past travels, including trips to Las Vegas, Baltimore and Puerto Rico, but Tuesday marked his first time trying fishing and other activities offered through Adventure Club.</p><p>"This one was mostly exciting," Stanley said. "Fishing needs to be a new thing right now."</p><p>Besides fishing, Adventure Club also offers kayaking and archery to the campers, who are in the Park District's special recreation program for people with intellectual or developmental disabilities. The idea is to offer activities that might otherwise be difficult to enjoy casually because they cost too much or the equipment is harder to use. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-340000" name="image-340000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9ace0a9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6910x3878+0+365/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7d%2Faa%2F812b9f3a445c85730677d86f049c%2Fadventureclub-260708-001-kayaks-skyline.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2defb1c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6910x3878+0+365/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7d%2Faa%2F812b9f3a445c85730677d86f049c%2Fadventureclub-260708-001-kayaks-skyline.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e71f7b1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6910x3878+0+365/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7d%2Faa%2F812b9f3a445c85730677d86f049c%2Fadventureclub-260708-001-kayaks-skyline.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Campers kayak in Burnham Harbor during Adventure Club, the Chicago Park District’s Special Recreation program at Northerly Island on Tuesday, July 7, 2026. The program offered participants a chance to reconnect with nature. At first, it, offered only kayaking, said Eileen Guinane, a Special Olympics administrator and 20-year employee. </p><p>"We started with the kayaking, and when we saw how beautiful it was back here and how much fun our guys had learning and being exposed to new activities, we kind of expanded and added the fishing and the archery," Guinane said.</p><p>The program has become so popular that it has routinely filled up each summer, with camps from across the city rotating through — and some who apply being turned away. Introducing participants to outdoor recreation beyond traditional sports helps broaden their experiences, he said.</p><p>"It's nice being able to bring something that they only get to do when we bring it to them," Fox said. entries.title: Man charged with handing girlfriend gun, encouraging suicide before she shot herself
entries.summary: <p>A man appeared in court Tuesday on charges alleging he encouraged his girlfriend's suicide before handing her the loaded gun with which she fatally shot herself.</p><p>Mario Laboy, 49, is charged with three felony counts of inducement to commit suicide in connection to the July 4 shooting in Portage Park that left Martha Rodriguez, 46, dead, according to the Cook County state's attorney's office.</p><p>Cook County Judge Luciano Panici Jr. ordered Laboy released while awaiting trial.</p><p>According to court documents prepared by prosecutors, Laboy arrived around midnight to Rodriguez's home in the 5000 block of West Sunnyside Avenue. Prosecutors said they had been dating for several years.</p><p>More than two hours later, he told her he was going to break up with her, prosecutors said. </p><p>Doorbell surveillance video shows Laboy walking to his car while Rodriguez remained on her porch, prosecutors said. </p><p>She then began texting him about suicide, prosecutors said. At that point, he allegedly told her that if she was going to hurt herself, not to "half-step," prosecutors said.</p><p>After more texts and an eight-minute phone call, Laboy allegedly returned to her porch around 3:07 a.m.</p><p>“Here you go. Do it," he was caught saying on nearby surveillance camera audio, according to prosecutors. "Put it in your mouth. Do it.”</p><p>A gunshot is heard on the audio before he screams and her children wake up, prosecutors said. When police arrived, Laboy led them to the porch where they recovered a revolver near her foot and started rendering aid, prosecutors said. She was taken to Advocate Lutheran General Hospital and pronounced dead.</p><p>Her death was ruled a suicide in the autopsy, prosecutors said. Laboy later admitted to police that he "may have handed her the gun," prosecutors said.</p><p>The Cook County public defender's office wasn't immediately able to comment.</p><p>Prosecutors said that Laboy previously faced a domestic violence charge in Tennessee but that the charge was dismissed in 2011.</p><p>Laboy is due in court again on July 23.</p><p><i>If you’re experiencing a mental health crisis, dial </i><b><i>988</i></b><i> to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. It’s open 24/7 and in Illinois still offers LGBTQ+ counselors. The Trevor Project also runs an around-the-clock youth hotline at 1-866-488-7386 and a </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.thetrevorproject.org/get-help/" target="_blank" ><i><u>text/chat</u></i></a><i> option.</i></p>

entries.title: Bob Biebel, Chicago police officer who met his wife on the beat, dies at 77
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Bob and Joan Biebel met on the job, as Chicago police officers, and things progressed slowly, as love stories go.</p><p>"I chased him for eight years before I finally made him surrender at City Hall," Joan Biebel said with a laugh.</p><p>"I wore high heels, and he had to park at the cheap parking lot three blocks away," she said. "Our reception was at McDonald's for a cup of coffee."</p><p>Mr. Biebel kept their courtship close to the vest.</p><p>"He and I were partners for years — I had no idea they were dating," recalled retired police officer Bobby Stevens. "Policemen sometimes are like old women, gossip wise. What's that phrase from World War II ... 'Loose lips sink ships.'"</p><p>The couple was occasionally paired in the same beat car early in their careers before they took on separate duties. </p><p>They had a daughter and named her Annie.</p><p>After 38 years on the job, Mr. Biebel retired in 2010 as a lieutenant with a special victims unit working the West Side.</p><p>With more time on his hands, Mr. Biebel joyfully watched his daughter's career as a consultant blossom.</p><p>She traveled regularly for work, and Mr. Biebel loved picking her up at O'Hare Airport. He didn't mind heavy traffic. It meant more time with his daughter while driving her home to her Downtown apartment.</p><p>Mr. Biebel died June 17 from natural causes, his family said. He was 77.</p><p>Hours before he died, he and his wife — foodies who loved exploring Chicago restaurants — hosted friends for dinner at their Sauganash home.</p><p>"He died in his sleep ... an Irish goodbye," his wife said. "I miss him very much, and I wish I was going out to dinner with him tonight. But I am very lucky. I have my daughter and my grandsons, and I had all those years with him."</p><p>Mr. Biebel was born on July 30, 1948, to Paul Biebel Sr. and Eleanor Sweeney Biebel. He was a mailman and a Big Ten basketball referee. She was a homemaker.</p><p>Mr. Biebel was the seventh of nine siblings. He had a wry smirk and a fondness for stirring things up.</p><p>"Dinner table rules were strictly enforced by our father, who was hard of hearing but could read lips," said Mr. Biebel's sister Rosemary Schulter. "So what you'd have to do is look down at your dinner plate to talk to someone across the dinner table, and Bobby knew how to upset the apple cart. He'd look at his plate and say something to antagonize someone and then of course the other kid who retaliated would get in trouble."</p><p>Mr. Biebel attended Our Lady of Lourdes grammar school, St. George High School in Evanston and DePaul University, where he studied accounting.</p><p>He worked as an accountant before following in the footsteps of two older siblings who became police officers.</p><p>He never fully gave up accounting, though. While on the police force, he scheduled his vacation during tax season to do accounting work with a firm with which he had a long-standing relationship.</p><p>"Bob epitomized what our mother and father taught us — work hard and do your job well," said his brother Paul Biebel, a former chief judge of the Cook County Criminal Court.</p><p>Mr. Biebel served as a sounding board for many young police officers and happily showed them how to use data to assist in police investigations, his wife said.</p><p>He was also a voracious reader and served as the glue for groups of friends he made dating back to childhood, his family said.</p><p>In recent years, Tom Corcoran talked to Mr. Biebel twice a day. They grew up near each other in a North Side neighborhood thick with large Irish families.</p><p>"He was a true character," said Corcoran, who caddied with Mr. Biebel, as well as actor Bill Murray, at Indian Hill Country Club in Winnetka when they were kids. "I reach for my phone to talk to him, and he's not there."</p><p>Mr. Biebel is survived by his wife, his daughter, Annie Lewandowski, and two grandsons. </p><p>Services have been held.<br></p>

entries.title: Sophie Cunningham finger paints a vivid picture of MAGA mindset
entries.summary: <p>Unlike you, I've actually been to a WNBA game. Ten years ago, at the invite of a Chicago Sky publicist. I thought it would be a fun outing for myself and my wife, and it was, in a low-key way. The crowd was small but enthusiastic. The action on the court was spirited. We had great seats — little tables on the floor behind the basket, in fact. We got free popcorn, and an orange-and-white basketball signed by the lanky Sky star at the time, Elena Delle Donne, who powered the team past the Seattle Storm, 92-88.</p><p>The game did not create in me a fervent interest in women's basketball. Which is no insult to women's sports. I'm not captivated by the men's NBA either.</p><p>But even I have noticed the ongoing saga of Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark, whose presence has supercharged the league. Her opponents seem to really hate her, because of — and I base this on my professional research, not personal bias, so don't blame me for these options — 1) her raw talent; 2) her $28 million contract with Nike; 3) her heterosexual orientation; 4) her white race; or 5) all four.</p><p>As a result Clark gets poked in the eye more than Curly Howard of the Three Stooges, and she is constantly being bludgeoned to the floor while refs gaze at the ceiling, if Instagram is any guide.</p><p>All of which could still be safely left to the sports pages. But Instagram has a way of holding your face in certain cultural moments, and Sunday my feed was inexplicably filled with Clark's teammate, Sophie Cunningham, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7395139/2026/06/25/sophie-cunningham-pointing-dewanna-bonner/" target="_blank" >pointing her finger.</a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Fans tonight already asking Sophie to pose for photos with the point 🫵<a href="https://x.com/hashtag/WNBAonUSA?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#WNBAonUSA</a> | Fever 🔥 <a href="https://t.co/y49UHEHgm9">pic.twitter.com/y49UHEHgm9</a></p>— USA Sports (@usasports) <a href="https://x.com/usasports/status/2069926231995191367?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 24, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>That's it. Pointing. At an opponent. In a very cool, focused manner.</p><p>Perhaps you've seen it. Perhaps some background is in order.</p><p>In a June 22 game, Clark was issued a technical foul after scuffling with Phoenix Mercury forward DeWanna Bonner. The call caused Cunningham to calmly point at Bonner, with an "I see you" look. Bonner started raging, and pointing herself, and demanding Cunningham stop pointing at her, prompting Cunningham to keep pointing, her face serene, rhythmically wagging her finger.</p><p>It might have been another dust mote in the media whirlwind. But the image gained traction online, and on June 30 <a class="Link" href="https://www.blogger.com/blog/post/edit/3972382144120426476/424682614544529065#" target="_blank" >the White House jumped in, </a>tweeting Cunningham talking about the incident on a podcast, paired with Donald Trump, also pointing — because everything has to be about him.</p><p>Now Cunningham's is the finger that launched a thousand memes.</p><p>Cunningham crossing the Delaware in place of George Washington. Cunningham as Helen of Troy. Cunningham at the water's edge, ordering a boatload of dodgy-looking refugees to "Go the f--- home."</p><p>Why? Well, again theories: Cunningham is 1) tall and blond, in the mold of the Fox News feminine ideal; 2) she's from Missouri, which led some to assume she's conservative, though there's no sign of that; 3) she's white, admonishing a Black player, causing some on Instagram to decide she's calling out DEI; 4) apparently straight, in a sport where that isn't always the case.</p><p>Cue that patented mind-reading trick the right has perfected: Cunningham's viral moment was deemed a finger in the eye of sputtering liberals. </p><p>"Why does Sophie Cunningham trigger the left so much?" asks a comment on Facebook with over 3,600 likes, providing zero examples of the supposed doorjamb-gnawing liberal outrage. "Sophie Cunningham is strong, talented, confident, and fearless — the kind of woman who refuses to bow down to woke nonsense or political correctness. While the radical left pushes its anti-woman agenda and tries to redefine strength, Sophie represents excellence, hard work, and real femininity. She shows young women that success comes from talent, grit, discipline, and determination — not victimhood, handouts, or special treatment. God bless Sophie Cunningham for showing the world what strong, accomplished American women look like. The left can’t stand her because she represents everything their failed ideology can’t produce."</p><p>As a designated representative of bleeding heart liberality (it's true; the Conservative Crusader once dubbed me "the king of left-wing lunacy in the Windy City"), I just want to state plainly that, before the political nonsense came pouring in like an overflowing toilet, I thought Cunningham's point was a boss move. I approve of Cunningham having Clark's back and particularly like what Cunningham said when reporters asked for her reaction to the White House putting her finger through its megaphone.</p><p>"I think everyone around the world is posting it," she said Friday, diplomatically. "Every company has done it. They also get on board. I don't think twice about it. I think they’re just another group who is posting about it.”</p><p>To not think twice about the endless howl of grievance echoing across this country — must be nice.</p>
